page: Amazon Web Services m6gd.2xlarge is an arm64 general-purpose instance powered by the AWS Graviton2 processor using ARMv8 Neoverse-N1 microarchitecture. The instance features 8 dedicated vCPUs mapped directly to 8 physical cores clocked at 2.5 GHz, without simultaneous multithreading. It provides 32.0 GB of system memory, matching a balanced 1:4 vCPU-to-RAM ratio of 4.0 GB per core. For I/O performance, it includes 474 GB of direct-attached NVMe SSD instance storage alongside a 2 Gbps baseline network bandwidth running on the AWS Nitro hypervisor.

Benchmark results demonstrate consistent multi-threaded throughput balanced by modest single-threaded processing. The stress-ng multi-core CPU score of 12,131.32 and Geekbench multi-core score of 5,299 fall into the average range across tested hardware, while Geekbench single-core performance (909.0) and bzip3 decompression (6.54 GB/sec) exhibit lower single-thread velocity. The server excels in caching and consistent memory bus operations, recording 472.98 GB/sec in small-block cached read tests and 121.9 GB/sec in uncached block reads. Application benchmarks show solid transactional capacity, reaching 9.83 million Redis SET operations per second and 9.71 GB/sec of static web serving throughput.

From a cost-efficiency perspective, the inclusion of direct-attached NVMe storage eliminates separate block storage fees for workloads that rely heavily on fast scratchpad or ephemeral data. However, the absence of x86 vector instructions like AVX-512 restricts performance in intensive AI or floating-point compute, as evidenced by low LLM inference rates. The m6gd.2xlarge is best suited for balanced enterprise workloads requiring low-latency local storage, such as caching nodes, microservices architectures, relational database replicas, CI/CD compilation, and web serving fleets.

Operating on the AWS Nitro hypervisor with a 2 Gbps network baseline, the architecture avoids simultaneous multithreading to ensure predictable core execution. Benchmarks show balanced multi-threaded performance, with Geekbench multi-core reaching 5,299 and Redis SET operations achieving 9.83 million ops/sec. While single-thread speeds and specialized machine learning inference are modest due to core frequency and lack of vector acceleration, the local high-speed disk provides significant qualitative cost efficiency by eliminating attached block storage overhead.
